chapter_theme: The first eighteen poems of the maruthakkali (66 to 83), sung as the wife's sulk against the husband's courtesans: nearly every poem opens with a pond, field or bee scene addressed to the 'man of the town', runs three refrains that set his oaths and go-betweens (bard, charioteer, washerwoman, brahmin) against the marks other women left on him, and closes with a bitter or yielding turn; one poem (76) is a kalavu exchange about gossip, and the last four make the little son the go-between, whom the courtesans also claim.

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the women he goes to

pairs.situation: he leaves the house for the women of the town
he spends his nights with women who receive him

pairs.scene: பண்டு தாம் மரீஇய பூம் பொய்கை மறந்து
pairs.situation: he forgets the wife he once lived with

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the bee of her own town's fields and pond, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

comparisons.tenor: the husband who leaves his wife for other women

66.reading: The wife tells the man of the town where the striped bee, after the blue lilies and the musk of the rutting elephant, spends the night in the jasmine of lovers' hair and forgets the pond it once haunted, that the gossip of his new wedding, his bathing and his dancing with other women was no grief to her but his own glory brought to her door at dawn, and that she has had his grace: his charioteer, crying that he is late, keeps the chariot yoked.
66.nuance: Every refrain thanks him for an injury: the scent of his wedding garland reaching her at dawn, the ornaments he has not even rearranged, the beauty of his revelry she is allowed to see. The close turns the visit into the last insult, since the chariot is never unyoked and he is only passing between houses.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband has taken a new woman and the wife sulks

comparisons.tenor: the Vaiyai in flower-laden flood, like the earth wearing a garland
the slender women he has embraced
the friend's bright brow

67.reading: The wife tells her friend that whenever the man of the walled town on the flooding Vaiyai comes back showing the wounds and marks of other women's garlands, paste and teeth, she says she will sulk, quarrel and turn cold, but the moment he is seen her helpless heart says it will join him; can those whose heart goes over to the enemy carry out what they planned?
67.nuance: The three refrains set her vow (என்பேன்மன், 'I would say') against what the heart does at the sight of him. The close calls the heart a traitor (அறைபோகு நெஞ்சு), a word from siege warfare: the fortress is given up from inside. The opening praise of the Vaiyai town that no enemy but its own flood attacks quietly sets up that siege.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's resolve to sulk at his whoring

comparisons.tenor: the poets who gather new words, like counsellors to a ruler
poets as ploughmen working with the tongue
the wife, unused like a garland kept in a casket
his embrace, real only while it lasts

68.reading: The wife tells the man of the walled town, where poets plough with the tongue, water the field of the ear with old sayings and harvest new words like counsellors to a king, that she will not blame the women who rattled her door at his signal, nor the talk that his chest cures every sulk, nor the charioteer asking street by street for the house he entered, she who saw his bard come in blessing the wedding house: his embrace, when he comes home, is for her like wealth won in a dream, gone on waking.
68.nuance: Each refrain asks 'shall I blame them?' and answers with what she herself has become: at war with her own shoulders, a garland left unworn in its casket. The opening simile of poets as tongue-ploughmen makes the town a place of fine words, which is the husband's own art.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulk at his many women

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the girl he has taken up

pairs.situation: he goes about with the new girl
he displays her openly as if she were his wedded wife
he made her bathe with him in the stream

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the swan of her own town's pond, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

comparisons.vehicle: ஓது உடை அந்தணன் எரி வலம் செய்வான்
comparisons.tenor: the swan circling the lotus with its mate
the bride's eyes
the husband parading his new woman

69.reading: The wife tells the man of the flooded town, where the swan with its graceful mate goes round the lone lotus as a Veda-reciting brahmin goes round the fire with his shy bride, that he stood to be blamed by the girl who took his heart in the street, left his charioteer to wait for her and made her bathe with him in the stream, and now comes pretending humility to say that she is weak and without restraint: let him do what he has planned and remember her only when those who love him tire.
69.nuance: Each refrain catches him doing one thing and saying another (துணிந்தது பிறிது ஆக, நெஞ்சத்த பிற ஆக). The opening wedding simile is pointed: the bird pair parades like a newly married couple, which is how he goes about with his new woman.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's new woman and his false humility

iraicchi.act: the hen swan, missing her mate for a moment, panics, runs to his false likeness and is shamed when he comes
iraicchi.sense: a wife who loses her husband even briefly is as anxious as the bird, so his long desertion is the greater cruelty

comparisons.tenor: the colour of the pond
the noises that break her sleep

70.reading: The wife tells the man of the town where a young hen swan, losing sight of her mate behind a lotus leaf, runs gladly to the moon's reflection in the water and then, meeting her mate, hides ashamed among the flowers, that since he left her, the eyes that had not slept for days, that wept without end and touched only her son, can at last close, only to be woken by his wedding drums, the dance of his kin and the bells of his chariot horses; let all of it wake her, so long as his bard with the lute does not come into her house.
70.nuance: The refrains reverse the usual complaint: his desertion is what lets her sleep, and his celebrations are what break it. Line 20 (மெல்லியான் செவி முதல் மேல்வந்தான் காலை போல்) is obscure; the sense of the close does not depend on it.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's new marriage and the wife's sulk

comparisons.tenor: the lotus opening with dew on one side
the fragrance of his chest
his coming once a year

71.reading: The wife tells the man of the town where, as the sun climbs, the lone lotus opens with dew on one side like the face of a woman who weeps in a sulk and laughs when her husband bows to her feet, that the charioteer who swore she was his only wife, the bard who swore on his lute and the friend who praises his virtues have not come to see his wounds, bangle scars and scented chest; she will not sulk, he may come in, but his coming once a year is like a drizzle that cannot satisfy paddy withering in the sheath for want of rain.
71.nuance: Each refrain names a go-between who vouched for him and asks why that witness does not come now to see the evidence on his body. The opening simile shows the reconciliation she will not perform: tears on one side, laughter on the other.

thinai_evidence.note: his whoring and her refusal to sulk

comparisons.tenor: the lotus bud opening

72.reading: The wife tells the man of the town where the lotus bud opens when a mango's young fruit touches it, like the face of a girl on a swan-down pillow coaxing a sulking parrot with a little milk in a bowl, that his bard, his washerwoman go-between and his brahmin flatterer surely sent him to show her his nail-scarred lip, the lac on his chest and the dust of women's hair; she is crushed, but enduring this pain is less base for her than forgetting the past and welcoming him whenever he appears.
72.nuance: The three go-betweens (bard, washerwoman, brahmin) are named one per refrain, each mocked as if he had ordered the husband to bring the evidence home. Her final choice is dignity over reconciliation.

thinai_evidence.note: the marks of other women on him

comparisons.tenor: the lotus opening
his whoring that is never satisfied

73.reading: The wife tells the man of the town where the lotus opens like the face of a woman drinking cool wine from a shining silver bowl, that he used to come assuring her he was blameless whenever no one accused him, as long as his crushed garland, the smeared paste on his chest and the cloth torn in the women's dance did not speak; his whoring, endless as the sea that no water fills, keeps him busy soothing sulking women every day, and she will not be fooled again by his lies.
73.nuance: The refrains depend on what she finds on him, not on what anyone tells her: the garland, the paste and the torn cloth are the witnesses. The last line (தோலாமோ நின் பொய் மருண்டு) can be read as 'shall I lose, bewildered by your lies?' and is taken here as a refusal.

thinai_evidence.note: his whoring and the wife's refusal

ullurai.tenor: the husband and his succession of women

pairs.situation: he leaves her for another before the day is out
he comes back to the fine house only after his rounds

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the bee of her own town's fields, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

comparisons.tenor: the lotus, perfect as if made by hand
the women who trust him though they see his lack of grace
his chariot hunting women

comparisons.vehicle: பொய்கைப் பூ புதிது உண்ட வரி வண்டு
comparisons.tenor: the husband moving from woman to woman

74.reading: To the man of the town where the striped bee, newly fed on pond flowers and the neythal of the backwater, moves on to the field lotus and its stamens, the wife says that the bard who praises him as loving and just is deluded, the women who trust his words though they see his lack of grace are deluded as those who drink poison knowing it kills, he is deluded who joins one woman at forenoon, leaves her at noon and looks for others in the afternoon, and his chariot, that the town laughs at as a net for big-eyed women, is more deluded than he.
74.nuance: The four refrains share one verb (ஏமுற்றான், ஏமுற்றார், ஏமுற்றாய், ஏமுற்றன்று), and the last falls on the chariot, an object, as if it were the most besotted of all. The morning-noon-afternoon schedule of line 10 and 11 mirrors the bee's flower-to-flower course.

thinai_evidence.note: his round of women and her contempt

comparisons.tenor: the startled birds crying in the trees

75.reading: The wife tells her friend, who watches her and grieves, that she does not grieve that the man of the rich town, where birds startled by girls at play fly into the trees crying as if to tell their kin what the girls did to them, loves new women as if every day were a wedding: when she would ask why he comes late, guests arrive and she forgets; when she sulks at his faded flowers, he comes to soothe her and she fears his false oaths; when she calls him a whoremonger, he hugs their son and pretends to sleep; so her sulk dies each time, and bearing it, she says, is her duty.
75.nuance: Three moves defeat her sulk: the duty to receive guests, the fear of making him swear falsely, and the son he holds as a shield while feigning sleep (பொய் துயில்). The birds that cry to their kin about the girls' raid are her opposite: they complain, she will not. The last line (நோவென்) can be read 'I grieve' or 'I do not grieve'; the reading follows line 12 (நோவேன்).

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulk and how it is defeated

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, smooth as bamboo

76.reading: The friend answers the girl who blames her for the town's talk about the man who gazed at her ornaments, followed her bathing, painted lines on her and bowed at their house: the talk came from his own attentions to the girl, the sedge doll from the sea, the flowers from the pond, the sugarcane drawn on her shoulder, yet she would not see that gossip is false and scolded the friend instead; now, the friend says, if the town has already done what their kin would do at the wedding, what is left for them to do?
76.nuance: The close turns the gossip into a wedding announcement: the town has published the match before the families have, so the only step left is marriage. The speaker and addressee are inferred; the poem's 'you' and 'we' could also be read the other way round, with the girl answering the friend.

thinai_evidence.note: a secret love exposed by gossip, before marriage

comparisons.tenor: the lotus dropping dew on the buds
her pale eyes
her dark hair

77.reading: The wife tells the man of the town where a lone lotus between two buds, touched by a bird, drops dew on them like a woman who bows her head grieving for her lover and lets tears fall on her breasts, that she does not ask back the beauty, the sleep and the flowered hair he took from her, if only she could be spared the taunt 'his woman', the complaints of the women he wrongs and his bard asking at her door for his other houses; but can she keep the resolve not to touch his chest, when her heart, an enemy living with her, rushes out at the sight of him?
77.nuance: The three refrains give up her own losses to ask only that the public shame stop. The close names the heart as an enemy who shares her house (உடன் வாழ் பகை), so her restraint (நிறை) is lost before any battle.

thinai_evidence.note: her vow of sulking and his other houses

ullurai.tenor: the husband who leaves the wife and returns at his convenience

pairs.situation: he quarrels with the household and goes off
he comes back when the trouble at home has passed

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the bee of her own town's lotus fields, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

comparisons.tenor: the bees leaving the flooded flower for another pond
the bees returning when the flood recedes
her beauty fading when he leaves
his presence to her, in his own boast
the wife withering
his forced embrace

78.reading: The wife tells the man of the town where a pair of bees, angry when the flood bends their lotus, leave for another pond as people flee to the king's shade when an enemy comes and return when he has quelled it, that he comes to her house wearing the proof of other women while claiming that her beauty withers when he leaves and blooms when he returns, like a flower that opens to the sun or a field that lives by rain; enough: those who desire him and those who love him are different, and his embrace, forced open like a bud in the hand, has no charm for her in the cold dew.
78.nuance: The three refrains quote his own boast about her dependence (each a simile of his: her beauty, the sun-flower, the rain-field) and answer each with the evidence he carries. The puram simile of the opening, a people sheltering under a king, makes the bee's return a return of subjects, which is how he sees her.

thinai_evidence.note: his other women and her refusal

comparisons.tenor: the paddy ear on the lotus petal
the son's red mouth

79.reading: The wife tells the man of the town, where one bright ear of paddy leaning on a lotus petal looks like the jewel on a dancer's brow, not to come here and take up their son: the boy's wet mouth will wash away the sandal paste, his hands will pull the pearl chain and the garland by which the other women marked him, and they will be angry; let him stop praising the boy with lies, leave the doorway, give the son back and go to them.
79.nuance: Her argument is mock concern for the other women: the child would undo their marks. So the son, usually the way back into the house, becomes the reason to send him away.

thinai_evidence.note: his other women and the wife's refusal

comparisons.tenor: the moon, called a child for the child

80.reading: The mother tells her little son, whom she calls her charioteer as he drags his toy elephant, that his tottering walk, his sweet 'attatta' and showing him the moon are a joy, but a pain when she sees the loosened bangles, the wasting and the stretch-marks of the women his father has used and turned his back on; still, she says, when he pulls the earring from her ear she will watch him swing on his father's broad chest among the garland and the bees, while the strangers' eyes look away.
80.nuance: The pity is aimed at the father's discarded women, whose state warns her of her own. Lines 1 to 3 (the three-strand ornament, கயம் தலை) are difficult and the reading of them is tentative.

thinai_evidence.note: the father's whoring seen through the son

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the little son

comparisons.vehicle: ஆல் அமர் செல்வன் அணி சால் பெரு விறல்
comparisons.tenor: the child toddling in his ornaments
hearing the child's words
the husband coming when the house is unguarded
the husband's false charges from afar
the husband going to his son

81.reading: In a dialogue, the wife watches their son toddle in the yard pulling his toy chariot, bright as the young son of the god under the banyan, and asks him to repeat the words the 'mothers' in the big street taught him; the husband pleads that the bard babbled them and the boy will not let them go, she answers that he came like thieves after the army has left and must go, standing in the wind with another woman's hair-dust on his cloth; and he ends that, if nothing is refused, he will take up his father's namesake and come like a cow to where its calf is tied.
81.nuance: The street women (ஞாயர், 'mothers') have taught the child words, so the boy carries the other houses into hers in his speech. The speakers shift without notice; the division of lines 16 to 37 between wife and husband is a reading, and ஏனாதிப்பாடியம் (line 17) is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the other woman's traces and his plea of innocence

comparisons.tenor: her breasts swelling with milk
the woman's tears
the other woman seizing the father

82.reading: The wife asks the woman who took their son round the temples why she kept him so long while her breasts swelled with milk, and hears that the boy went into the house of the woman his father first loved, who adorned him with ivory and wept pearls of tears, and then into the house of the next, who kissed him, asked 'what am I to you?' and called his father's whoring unworthy; the wife cries for a stick, tells the boy how that woman seizes his father like a kite and scars him with nails, and orders the attendant to keep the boy from such houses: that is her job.
82.nuance: The father's women speak to the son as stepmothers would, and one of them blames the father in the wife's own words. The poem is the wife's jealousy turned on her husband's past through what her child saw.

thinai_evidence.note: the father's women seen through the son's visit

comparisons.tenor: the women's eyes at the window
the father's arrival after the son's

83.reading: The wife asks why the boy, taken out to play in the sandy street, stayed away so long while her milk ran; she is told that as he came home with his toy chariot of palmyra fruit, women at the windows, eyes trembling like blue lilies in the wind, cried that the festival of the god's son had begun, came down and claimed him for the night to ease the loneliness his shameless father left them in; then the father too arrives, with ornaments and scars, and she says it is like a spear thrust into a burn.
83.nuance: The festival of Murugan, the son of the god under the banyan, is the women's excuse to hold the son, who is himself compared to that god's child in poem 81. The son first and the father next bring the same marks home, so the wound is given twice.

thinai_evidence.note: the father's women and his return with their marks

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: first the attendant who took the son out, then the husband

links.note: Kalittokai 67's three refrains say 'I would say I will sulk' (புலப்பேன் யான் என்பேன்மன்) and the heart says it will join him; Kural 1284 has the woman go to sulk and her heart go to unite (ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன்மன் ... கூடற்கண் சென்றது).
links.teaches: The Kural's couplet is one turn of a song the Kalittokai performs three times with three different marks on the man's body, and the Kalittokai names the heart's act outright as treason (அறைபோகு), showing that the couplet's quiet split between woman and heart was heard as betrayal from within.

links.note: Kural 1254 says she used to call herself restrained (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன்) but desire breaks out in public; Kalittokai 77 asks whether restraint (நிறை) is easy for one who lives with an enemy, her own heart.
links.teaches: The Kural blames desire in general for breaking restraint, while the Kalittokai wife places the failure in a precise moment, the sight of the unfaithful husband at her door, so the same loss of நிறை turns from a lover's confession into a wronged wife's helplessness against her own grievance.

links.note: Kural 1143 welcomes the gossip the whole town knows, because it gives as if already got what is not yet got; Kalittokai 76 ends that if the town has done what their kin would do at the wedding, nothing is left to do.
links.teaches: Both turn alar from shame into a kind of marriage, and together they show the two uses of the same claim: the Kural lover savours the gossip as a foretaste, while the Kalittokai friend uses it as an argument that the wedding is already public and must now follow.

links.note: Kural 1192 likens a lover's grace to the rain that sustains those who live by it; Kalittokai 71 likens the husband's once-a-year visit to a drizzle that cannot satisfy paddy withering for want of rain.
links.teaches: The Kural's rain stands for grace given in its season, and the Kalittokai shows the same image under neglect: a token visit is not rain but drizzle, so the wife measures grace by its sufficiency, a test the Kural's simile assumes but does not state.

links.note: Kural 580 praises those who, wanting a refinement worth loving, see poison poured and drink it; Kalittokai 74 calls the women who trust the husband's words though they see his graceless ways deluded, like those who eat poison knowing it kills.
links.teaches: Knowingly swallowing poison is a mark of courtesy in the Kural and a mark of delusion in the Kalittokai, so the same act is judged by whom it is done for: forbearance toward a friend is refinement, forbearance toward a faithless lover is folly.

links.note: Kural 1215 says what was seen awake was sweet then, and the dream too is sweet while it is seen; Kalittokai 68 says the husband's embrace is like wealth won in a dream, different on waking.
links.teaches: The Kural's lover levels waking and dream, both sweet while they last, but the Kalittokai wife uses the dream to name a possession that vanishes, so the dream simile can console a parted lover or indict an unfaithful husband depending on whether the absence is chosen.

links.note: Natrinai 250: the man came near his son practising walking with his little chariot in the street (தேர் நடைபயிற்றும்) and his wife shied away saying 'who are you?'; Kalittokai 81: the son practises walking with his chariot in the yard (கால் வல் தேர் கையின் இயக்க, நடை பயிற்றா) while husband and wife argue over him.
links.teaches: The Natrinai gives the husband's side in one recoil, while the Kalittokai stages the whole quarrel around the same toddling child, so together they show the son with his toy chariot as the standing occasion for the husband's return in marutham, and the wife's refusal as a scene both anthologies expected.

links.note: In Akananuru 16 the wife finds a courtesan clasping their son in the chariot street and gently asks if she is his mother too; in Kalittokai 82 the son's visits to the father's women, who adorn and kiss him, make the wife call for a stick.
links.teaches: The same encounter of the son with his father's women draws grace from one wife and fury from another, showing that marutham poets used it to test the wife's karpu: the Akananuru wife proves her dignity by kindness, the Kalittokai wife her love by jealousy.

links.note: Kuruntokai 359: the friend shows the bard the man embracing his son on the bed and the wife embracing his back; Kalittokai 75: when she quarrels, he hugs the son and feigns sleep (புதல்வன் புல்லிப் பொய் துயில் துஞ்சும்).
links.teaches: Read together, the Kuruntokai's picture of a seemly household and the Kalittokai's account of the husband's tactic show that the son held in sleep was both the sign of reconciliation and the means of forcing it, and the wife in 75 knows it and yields anyway.

links.note: In Akananuru 66 the husband, on his way to a new wedding, lifts the crying son to his chest and gives up the wedding; in Kalittokai 79 the wife forbids him to take up the son, since the boy would wash off the other women's marks, and sends him back to them.
links.teaches: The husband's embrace of the son is the turning point of return in the Akananuru but is refused as a ruse in the Kalittokai, so the same gesture can end the husband's straying or be read by the wife as one more performance.

links.note: Akananuru 86 recalls a wedding of matrons pouring water with petals and paddy and the bride curled in her new cloth (கோடிக் கலிங்கத்து ஒடுங்கினள்); Kalittokai 69 compares the swan pair to a brahmin circling the fire with his shy bride shrunk in her cloth (கலிங்கத்துள் ஒடுங்கிய).
links.teaches: The shy bride in her new cloth is a shared formula, but the rite around her differs: the Akananuru wedding has matrons, water and paddy and no fire, while the Kalittokai sets her beside a Veda-reciting priest circling the fire, so the two anthologies record two wedding rites in Tamil country.

links.note: Purananuru 92 says a son's prattle keeps no tune and makes no sense, yet moves fathers to grace; in Kalittokai 80 the mother hears the son's sweet 'attatta' but the father is away with other women.
links.teaches: The puram poet's comparison assumes a father present to be moved by the prattle, and the Kalittokai shows the house where he is not, so the grace the prattle should draw from the father falls to the mother and is mixed with pain.

source_issues: kalittokai: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.

kalittokai:75 line 11: ஃ restored from the old encoding (flag repaired).
kalittokai:82 lines 6-35 and kalittokai:83 lines 8-31 are absent from sangamtamil.com (flag not_in_stc); our text has them and they were marked as they stand.
kalittokai:81 line 17 (ஏனாதிப்பாடியம்) and kalittokai:70 line 20 (மெல்லியான் செவி முதல் மேல்வந்தான் காலை போல்) are obscure; readings marked uncertain.
kalittokai:80 lines 1-3 (கயம் தலை மின்னும் கதிர் விடு முக் காழ்) are difficult; the reading of the child's ornament is tentative.
